--- title: "Statistical Modelling III" date: "2023-11-8" --- In our last class on multivariate analysis, we'll take on one of the more underappreciated elements of modeling: understanding if your model is good enough for prediction or inference. We'll spend a bit of time differentiating the uses of models as a means of understanding what it means to be a "good" model. ## Resources - [A practical guide to selecting models for exploration, inference, and prediction in ecology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecy.3336) by [@Tredennick2021] highlights the importance of understanding model performance before making inference on predictor effects. - [Model selection using information criteria, but is the “best” model any good?](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.13060) by [@Mac_Nally2018] highlights the importance of understanding model performance before making inference on predictor effects. - [Standards for distribution models in biodiversity assessments](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aat4858) by [@Araujo2019] highlights the importance of understanding model performance before making inference on predictor effects. ## Objectives By the end of today you should be able to: - Articulate three different reasons for modeling and how they link to assessments of fit - Describe and implement several test statistics for assessing model fit - Describe and implement several assessments of classification - Describe and implement resampling techniques to estimate predictive performance
